I'm ready to make a Monopoly decision.

I have $2166 and a pink monopoly with four houses on each property. The opponent has only $94 and two developed properties with four houses each. I am considering whether to trade or build.

The opponent has a hotel on Connecticut Avenue and another on Boardwalk. The bank has no houses left. Selling houses returns them to the bank.

The opponent cannot sell their hotels. Standard Monopoly rules require replacing a hotel with four houses, but the bank has none left. They also face even-build constraints on their light blue properties.

The opponent cannot downgrade their Connecticut hotel. They could sell one house from Oriental or Vermont to reach three houses, creating a two-house spread.

The opponent cannot sell houses from their light blue properties either. A hotel is worth five houses, so the difference between Connecticut Avenue and Oriental or Vermont would become two houses. That violates the even-building rule.

The opponent can sell houses from their red properties. They have two houses on Kentucky Avenue and three each on Indiana and Illinois Avenue. Red houses sell back for seventy-five dollars each.

The opponent's maximum liquidity is roughly $1,034. That figure includes cash, the $600 from selling red houses, and the $340 from mortgaging those properties.

I am now checking the exact rent schedule for my pink monopoly. St. Charles Place with four houses pays $625.

Virginia Avenue with four houses pays $700. St. Charles Place and States Avenue each pay $625. I am now checking whether the opponent can land on my pink properties from Kentucky Avenue.

The opponent cannot land on my pink properties from Kentucky Avenue in one roll. St. Charles Place sits too far around the board to reach within twelve spaces.

I am now mapping the spaces I will land on from Mediterranean Avenue. The next roll would hit Community Chest, Baltic Avenue, Income Tax, Reading Railroad, Oriental Avenue, Chance, Vermont Avenue, Connecticut Avenue, Jail, St. Charles Place, Electric Company, and States Avenue. I am now identifying which of these spaces pose the greatest threat.

Oriental Avenue with four houses pays $400. Vermont Avenue with four houses pays $400. Connecticut Avenue with a hotel pays $600. Reading Railroad is mortgaged and collects no rent. Income Tax costs $200. I have $2166.

I am weighing whether to build hotels on my pink properties. Each hotel costs one hundred dollars, so three hotels would cost three hundred dollars. The total rent increase would be four hundred fifty dollars. However, building hotels returns twelve houses to the bank.

I am now calculating the opponent's liquidation options if I build hotels. Twelve houses would return to the bank, allowing them to sell their Boardwalk hotel and Park Place houses. They could also sell their Connecticut hotel and light blue houses. Dark blue properties are worth only one hundred dollars each when sold back, so that path would raise minimal cash.

Selling a dark blue hotel returns four houses to the bank. Those houses can be sold back for one hundred dollars each, adding four hundred dollars in cash. The opponent could also sell their Park Place houses, adding another four hundred dollars. That totals eight hundred dollars from dark blue liquidation.

The opponent could raise roughly nine hundred dollars by selling all eight houses and mortgaging Park Place and Boardwalk. That liquidity would let them survive a pink rent hit and rebuild. The bank currently holds no houses, so they cannot liquidate dark blue or light blue buildings yet.

A single pink rent hit would not bankrupt the opponent. Virginia Avenue's $700 rent leaves them with $334 after selling red houses. St. Charles Place and States Avenue's $625 rent leaves them with $409. They can sell buildings and mortgage properties to pay rent.

A second pink rent hit could bankrupt the opponent. After paying Virginia Avenue's $700, they would need to mortgage a red property to cover the remaining $6. They would then be left with only $104 and stripped reds, so another pink hit would finish them unless they pass GO or find other cash.

I have decided not to build hotels or sell houses. Keeping the housing shortage frozen will prevent the opponent from liquidating their most valuable properties. I also will not unmortgage the Pennsylvania Railroad or Tennessee Avenue, since unmortgaging costs ten percent interest on the mortgage value.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad is not worthwhile. The opponent already owns the other three railroads, so there is no monopoly benefit. The rent would be only twenty-five dollars.

Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue would complete the orange monopoly for the opponent. They already own St. James and New York, both mortgaged. Trading it to them would give them a full set with no rent benefit.

I will not trade cash or Tennessee Avenue. Cash would help them survive Virginia Avenue's rent. Tennessee would complete their orange monopoly.

I will not trade Get Out of Jail Free cards. The opponent owns every property and has no assets I want, so trading offers no benefit. The only viable path is to keep four houses on all three pink properties and freeze the bank's housing supply, waiting for them to land on a pink twice or fail to pay rent. They are now on Kentucky Avenue and will roll next.

Rolling from Mediterranean Avenue would not land on any pink property. The main risks are light blue properties and a Chance card. An "Advance to Boardwalk" card would cost $2,000, but I have $2,166 and could survive without selling anything. I am now checking the rent for Park Place with four houses.

I now have $2,166, so I can pay the $1,300 rent on Park Place with four houses and the $2,000 rent on Boardwalk hotel without selling any buildings. Earlier I had only $1,966, which forced me to sell a house for Boardwalk. I will keep my current position and avoid building hotels or selling houses.

I am now considering whether to offer cash for Boardwalk to remove the $2,000 rent threat. The opponent would not accept a trade that gives them Boardwalk or light blue properties.
